ch.h:
You'll want to sit at the back. Everyone does, the first time. The back row of Courtroom Four has a radiator that knocks twice an hour, and from there you can watch the whole room without anyone catching you at it.

I sit at the front. Third row, left side, at the end, beside my wife. Nobody has asked me to move. Nobody has noticed I'm here, which is the one thing about being dead that turned out exactly as advertised.

Mira is wearing the grey dress. She bought it for her cousin's wedding and then decided it was too plain for her cousin's wedding. Sami is on her lap, though at six he is too long for it, and his shoes rest where my knee would be. Noor sits apart from them by the width of a handbag. She is ten. This year she has decided she is old enough to sit on her own, and I am in no position to tell her otherwise.

At two minutes past nine the side door opens and they bring him in.

I want to be fair to you, so I'll describe him fairly. He is well pressed. His shirt has been ironed by someone who irons for money. He wears a good steel watch, the kind that doesn't need to be looked at to be noticed, and he doesn't look at it. He walks the way men walk into meetings they have already won.

I never owned a watch. Mira used to say that people read a man's wrist before they read his face. She said it kindly, the first few times. I was late to my own wedding because a man at the bus stop needed help reading a letter from his son. Mira laughed about that for years. Then she stopped laughing about it, and then she stopped mentioning it, and I'm told that's the usual order.

"Murderer."

Noor says it. Not loudly. She says it the way she used to give answers in spelling tests: certain, and a little afraid of being right.

The accused stops. He looks at her for exactly as long as it takes the guard's hand to find his elbow. Then he sits down.

The clerk rises. She has a cold, and she reads around it.

"The State versus the accused. The charge is wilful murder. The deceased is" — she checks the paper — "known to his family as Eli."

At the defence table, Sal lowers his head, as if the clerk has made a small mistake and he is too polite to correct it.

I'll say this once so you don't think I'm sulking about it later. Sal is defending the man who killed me. He's wearing the blue tie he wore to my wedding, and he has knotted it into a thin, apologetic thing. For twenty years I was the one who tied it for him before anything important: the fat, perfect triangle we called the samosa. He would stand with his chin up like a boy getting his face washed, and complain the whole time.

Nobody has tied it for him in four years. You can tell.

"How does the accused plead?"

He stands. He buttons his jacket, which no one asked him to do.

"Not guilty," he says. He says it the way you'd tell a child the stove isn't hot: patiently, and certain you'll be proved right.

The judge is an old woman with reading glasses on a cord. She writes something down and doesn't look up. "Ms. Hale."

The prosecutor stands without hurry. She has no papers in her hands. That's the first thing I notice about her, and later I'll understand it was the most important thing.

"The State will not ask you to imagine a violent man," she says. "Look at him. You couldn't if you tried. He has never raised his voice in this building, and he won't. He pays his taxes early."

She lets that sit.

"He doesn't deny that he killed the deceased. He'll tell you so himself, and he'll be polite about it. He'll tell you the deceased asked him to. He'll tell you the family asked him to. The State will show you something simpler. He wanted a life that belonged to someone else. He was patient. And he took it one room at a time."

Mira's hand closes on Sami's shoe.

"The State will ask every witness one question," Hale says. "When did you last see Eli? You'll notice the answers don't agree. That isn't because anyone is lying. It's because he didn't die all at once."

She sits down. The radiator at the back knocks twice.

I told you to sit there.

The State's first witness is Inspector Varga, a heavy man who sits as if the chair has disappointed him before.

"Eight months ago," Hale says, "you received a report. Tell the court who made it."

"The deceased's wife, ma'am. She came into the station at one-forty in the morning. She was still dressed for a party. Earrings, the lot."

"What did she say?"

Varga checks his notebook, though he doesn't need to. "She said, 'My husband is gone. There's a man in my house.'"

The gallery shifts. Mira doesn't move at all.

"And when you went to the house?"

"The accused was at the kitchen table. Shirt and tie, at two in the morning. He was doing the household accounts. Bills in one pile, receipts in another." Varga turns a page. "I told him why we were there. He asked if he could finish the column he was on. I said no. He said that was fair, and stood up."

"Did he resist?"

"No, ma'am. He asked me to keep my voice down. Children asleep."

"Did you search the house?"

"The study. The deceased's desk, bottom drawer. It was full of old things. Game discs. A folder with a child's drawings, horses mostly, labelled HORSES, and then in brackets, BAD."

So that's where it went.

"Under the folder was an envelope, addressed to the wife. On the front it said, 'Open this if I die.' It was dated three years ago."

Hale takes the envelope from the clerk and gives it to him. "Read it, please. All of it."

I'd like to tell you I don't remember writing it. I remember the pen. It was one of Sami's, a green one that smelled of apples, because I couldn't find mine.

Varga puts on his reading glasses. He reads slowly, like a man carrying something full to the brim.

Mira,

If I ever die, and you're wondering whose fault it was, it was his. Don't let anyone tell you it was yours.

He isn't cruel. That's the worst part. You've met him already, and you liked him, and your sister likes him even more. He's good at parties. He knows what to say about cars. He'll pay the fees on the first of the month, and he'll never be late. Not once. Not even for something that matters.

I'm not writing this to stop him. I don't think I can anymore. I'm writing it so that when he's sitting in my chair, you'll remember someone sat in it before him. He was late for things. He drew terrible horses. He told the boy at the signal every morning that he was the luckiest man on the main road, and he meant it.

Tell Noor I didn't forget the last level.

And whatever he gives you, don't thank him. He'll think it means you wanted it.

I'm sorry I wasn't enough. I really did try to be.

E.

Varga folds the letter back along its old lines and hands it to the clerk.

Mira has a tissue in her hands. She unfolds it, smooths it on her knee, and folds it again into a smaller square. She does this four times. Noor watches her do it and doesn't help.

"Inspector," Hale says, "when did you last see Eli?"

"I never met him, ma'am."

"Thank you."

Sal stands. He has the letter's copy in front of him, and he's marked something on it in pencil.

"Inspector. The letter says, 'I'm not writing this to stop him.' Did I read that correctly?"

"Yes, sir."

"A man knows, three years before it happens, exactly who will kill him. He writes it down. And he writes that he won't stop it." Sal looks up. "In your experience, how often does a victim—"

"Objection," Hale says, without standing. "He's asking for speculation."

"Sustained."

"Withdrawn." Sal turns a page. "One more thing. That night, when you took the accused out of the house. Was anyone in the house afraid of him?"

Varga thinks. "The little boy came downstairs. Barefoot. All the noise had woken him."

"And?"

"He asked the accused to carry him back up to bed."

Sami, on Mira's lap, looks up at the sound of himself.

"Did the accused do it?"

"He asked my permission first," Varga says. "Then he did."

Noor's teacher, Mr. Abel, is a nervous man who apologises to the microphone when it squeals.

Hale holds up a drawing by its corners so the room can see. Crayon on school paper, wavy from the glue. Across the top, in careful capitals: MY FAMILY. Four figures on a green line of grass. A woman in a yellow dress. A girl with two plaits. A small boy with his arms out like an aeroplane. After the boy, the green line keeps going, empty, all the way to the edge of the page.

"Noor drew this at eight," Mr. Abel says. "The assignment was the people you live with. I asked her where her father was. She said he was at work. I told her she could draw him at work, if she liked." He clears his throat. "She said she didn't know what that looked like."

"Had she drawn her father before?"

"Many times. Her file goes back to her first year. At six she drew him lying on the floor next to her with a game controller in his hand." He blinks at the drawing. "She made him bigger than the house."

She used to draw on her stomach on the front-room rug, ankles crossed in the air. I drew horses for her. They had dog faces and too many knees, and she laughed until she got hiccups, then made me draw another so she could laugh again.

"When did you last see Eli, Mr. Abel?"

"At a parents' evening. Four years ago, perhaps. He stayed behind after everyone left and helped me stack the chairs." He looks unhappy. "Since then the fees have come by bank transfer."

Sal stands, and doesn't button his jacket.

"The fees. Were they ever late?"

"Never. The first of the month. The art programme, the trips, the extra maths. There's a fee for everything," Mr. Abel says, and then looks sorry he said it.

"Before four years ago. Were they late then?"

Mr. Abel looks at the floor. "Sometimes."

"Thank you."

Hale doesn't look at Sal, but she writes something down. I don't like that she writes something down.

The next witness is a young man of about seventeen, thin, in a borrowed jacket with the sleeves too short. When he was smaller he worked the traffic signal on the main road, selling flowers and cloths for windscreens. His name is Yusuf. He speaks to the floor.

"Every morning he bought me bread. Not money, bread. He said money was for my father, but bread was for me. He'd ask if I'd been to school. If I said no, he got angry. Not loud. He just held on to the bread until I promised."

Don't make it into something noble. It was bread. It cost less than the bus fare.

"He said a thing every morning," Yusuf goes on. "The same thing. He'd wind down the window and say, 'Yusuf, you're looking at the luckiest man on the main road.' Even when it rained. Even when his car made that noise."

"The defence will tell this court," Hale says, "that the deceased agreed to his own death. That he asked for it."

Yusuf looks up for the first time.

"No."

"Why are you sure?"

"Because a man who says he's lucky every morning doesn't ask to be killed. He'd have to stop saying it first."

"Did he stop?"

Yusuf thinks about it for a long time. "One morning the window stayed up."

"Did you knock?"

"I knocked."

"What happened?"

"The light changed."

"When did you last see Eli, Yusuf?"

"That winter. Five years. The winter my sister was born."

Sal stands. He looks at the boy for longer than a lawyer should, and I know he's deciding whether to ask the questions he has written down. He asks them anyway.

"In all those mornings. Did you ever see him buy anything for himself?"

"No, sir."

"His car made a noise, you said. Did it ever get fixed?"

Yusuf almost smiles. "No, sir."

"Did he look happy to you?"

"He looked tired, sir. Happy tired."

"And when the window stayed up. Do you blame him?"

"No, sir," Yusuf says. "I miss him."

He steps down. On his way past the defence table he slows, just slightly, the way you slow passing a shop window where something used to be on display.

"The State calls the wife of the deceased."

Mira lifts Sami off her lap and looks for somewhere to put him. Noor holds out her arms without being asked. The handbag's width between them closes. Sami settles against his sister and watches his mother walk to the stand.

She takes the oath with her chin up. Her mother taught her that. Her mother taught her a lot of things.

"Tell the court about your husband," Hale says.

Mira looks at her hands.

"He was late to our wedding," she says. "Did someone already say that? He was late because a man at the bus stop couldn't read. My father wanted to call it off. I told him if he called it off I'd marry Eli at the bus stop."

A few people in the gallery smile. She doesn't.

"He came home at five. Every day, five. He brought bread from the corner, still warm, and he ate the end of it on the stairs so I wouldn't see. He did the voices for Sami's bath duck. The duck had a wife, and the wife had opinions." Her mouth moves, nearly a smile. "He played that game with Noor every night. The two of them on the floor, shouting. He cried at films. Even the bad ones. Especially the bad ones."

The clerk brings an old console to the front of the court, its cable wrapped around it like a bandage. On the courtroom television a menu appears, with a tinny loop of music someone composed years ago to be cheerful forever.

SAVE FILE 1. TWO PLAYERS. FINAL STAGE.

Last played: four years and three months ago.

Noor isn't crying. She looks at the screen the way you look at a house you used to live in.

"The accused will tell this court," Hale says, "that your husband asked to die."

"That's a lie." It comes out of Mira fast, as if it's been waiting behind her teeth for eight months. "Eli wouldn't leave a party early in case the host felt bad. He wouldn't leave a stray cat in the rain. He would never, ever leave his children."

"Then why do you believe the accused killed him?"

Mira turns and looks at the accused for the first time. He looks back at her politely, the way you'd look at someone across a meeting table.

"Because he wanted what Eli had," she says. "The house. The chair at the head of the table. The children calling for him at night. He wanted to be the one we—" She stops. "He wanted us. And Eli was in the way."

"When did you last see Eli?"

This is the first question that takes her a long time.

"I don't know," she says.

"Take your time."

"I kept thinking he was just late. He was always late." She folds her hands. "I kept thinking he'd come home."

Hale lets the silence stand, and then sits.

Sal stands slowly. He and Mira have known each other for thirteen years. He gave a speech at their wedding. She has fed him dinner more times than either of them could count.

"Mira," he says.

"Counsel," the judge says.

"Ma'am." He looks at his notes, though I know he won't need them. "When you married, what did your husband earn?"

"Enough."

"Enough for what?"

"For us."

"And after Sami was born?"

She takes a moment. "Less than enough."

"Your sister's house. How many bedrooms?"

"Objection," Hale says. "Relevance."

"It goes to motive, Your Honour," Sal says. "The question in this courtroom is whose."

The judge looks at him over her glasses for a long moment. "I'll allow it. Briefly."

"Five," Mira says.

"And yours?"

"Two. Then."

"Did you ever ask your husband to dress better?"

"Every wife—"

"Did you?"

"Yes."

"To stand up straighter at gatherings? To speak up when your brothers-in-law talked about their work? To stop telling the bus-stop story at your mother's table?"

"It embarrassed—" She stops herself.

"It embarrassed him?"

Mira looks at the back wall, where the radiator is.

"It embarrassed me."

Sal waits. He's always been good at waiting. It's the only thing he was ever better at than me.

"My mother used to say a woman is seen through her husband," Mira says, to nobody in particular. "Like through a window. If the glass is dirty, people think the dirt is hers." She looks down at her hands as if she has only just noticed them. "I didn't know I'd said that out loud to him until I heard him repeat it to Noor."

She was tired. You would have been tired too. Four people in two rooms, and a sister who sends photographs of her new kitchen at eleven at night with no message, just the photograph. You'd have been tired, and you'd have said things.

"Did you know the accused," Sal asks, "before your husband's death?"

"Yes."

"For how long?"

"Some years."

"Did you ever bring him to your sister's gatherings?"

The gallery goes still. Mira's chin comes down a little.

"He was better at them," she says.

Someone behind me whispers something. I won't repeat it.

"Your mother's sixtieth birthday," Sal says. "Someone at that table said grown men don't play games. Who said it?"

"My sister."

"And what did you say?"

"I agreed with her." Very quietly. "Everyone was laughing."

Sal puts his notes down on the table. He doesn't look at them again.

"Mira. What did you want from him?"

She answers straight away, as if she's said it to herself in the dark many times and has only been waiting for someone to ask.

"I asked him for more. I never asked him for less of himself."

"Did you ever tell him that second part?"

She doesn't answer. The radiator knocks once and then, after a long time, again.

"The witness will answer," the judge says, not unkindly.

"I thought he knew," Mira says.

"No further questions."

Hale stands again, just for a moment.

"You said you didn't know when you last saw Eli. Tell the court when you knew he was gone."

Mira wipes her face with the side of her hand.

"At my sister's, eight months ago. My brother-in-law told the bus-stop story. As a joke. He does a voice for the man who couldn't read." She breathes. "Eli used to laugh at that story too. But he laughed like it was a good thing he'd done. And the man beside me laughed at him."

"What did you do?"

"I went home. I looked at the kitchen table with all the bills sorted into piles. Then I went to the police."

She steps down. When she gets back to the third row, Noor doesn't hand Sami back. Mira sits in the space between her daughter and the end of the row, the space where I am, and for a second I can't tell which of us is moving over.

After lunch it's the defence's turn. Sal stands, and for the first time today he buttons his jacket.

"I've known the deceased since we were nine," he says. "The first time I saw him, three boys had taken his lunch behind the school wall. When they'd finished, he asked if they wanted his apple too, because it seemed a shame to leave it out."

A few people laugh. Sal lets them.

"I loved him. I'm going to tell you the truth about him anyway, because he can't."

He walks to the middle of the floor.

"He was kind. Everyone in this room has said so, and they're right. He was also naive, in a way that cost the people around him. He lent money to anyone with a sad enough story, and never once got it back. He was passed over for promotion six years in a row, because every time there was credit to take, he gave it to whoever was standing nearest. He never asked for a raise. His car made a noise for nine years. He couldn't give his family a place to stand at their own relatives' tables. And he knew it. He lay awake doing sums on the ceiling."

You're nodding. Stop it.

"He didn't make his wife happy," Sal says. "He didn't make his children's school trips happen. He didn't, by the end, even make himself happy. So he went to the one man who could do what he couldn't, and he asked for help. Not to be hurt, Your Honour. To be relieved."

He turns, just slightly, toward the third row.

"The defence will show that this was planned for years, by both men, openly. And that the family didn't just know about it. They set the table for it."

The defence calls Mira's sister.

Dina comes to the stand in a coat the colour of good butter. She smiles at the judge as if they've met at a wedding.

"How would you describe the accused?" Sal asks.

"Honestly? Wonderful." She says it to the gallery. "Everyone said so. He was the first one at the door, the first one with a gift. He talked to my husband about property for an hour. My husband doesn't talk to anybody for an hour."

"And the deceased?"

She pauses, choosing a kind word. "Sweet."

"Did the family ever talk about him? About his shortcomings?"

"We all did. It was a joke, mostly. He took it so well. That was the thing about him, he took everything so well."

"Did anyone suggest he needed to change?"

"Everyone." She looks surprised by the question. "Mira most of all, to be fair to her. She'd been saying it for years."

In the third row, Mira doesn't move.

"At your mother's sixtieth," Sal says, "someone said grown men don't play games."

Dina laughs. "Oh, that was Mira. I only repeated it."

Hale stands for the cross-examination and doesn't approach the stand.

"Did you ever say any of this to the deceased directly?"

"Of course not," Dina says. "That would have been rude."

"When did you last see Eli?"

Dina opens her mouth and then closes it. She looks, for a moment, genuinely puzzled.

"I'm not sure I'd know," she says. "He was usually in the kitchen. Helping."

The last defence witness before the accused is a night guard named Anton. He wears his uniform to court because he's going straight to work afterwards, and he apologises for it twice.

"You worked in the accused's building."

"Eleven years, sir."

"Tell us about him."

"First in, last out." Anton says it the way you'd recite a man's address. "Most nights after nine. I'd walk him to the gate. He knew every manager's name, every deadline, every number on every floor. If someone was off sick, he took their work home. Never complained. Never once."

"The prosecution says he killed a man out of greed. To take what the deceased had."

Anton frowns as if the idea is a puzzle he can't find the edges of.

"Sir, I don't know what he'd have been taking. He didn't need to kill anybody to get anything. He was already giving everything he had." He shakes his head. "There wasn't anything left over to be greedy with. He ate the same sandwich at his desk for four years."

"Thank you, Anton."

Hale rises.

"Mr. Anton. Did the accused ever talk about his family?"

"Oh, yes, ma'am. All the time. The school fees. Class rankings. The new house."

"Did he ever say their names?"

Anton opens his mouth to answer. He thinks. He thinks for longer than he expected to.

"He mentioned the fees, ma'am."

"When did you last see Eli?"

"I don't remember, ma'am," Anton says, and looks apologetic about this too.

"The defence calls the accused."

He walks to the stand the way he walked in this morning. He takes the oath and sits, and he doesn't touch the glass of water the clerk has poured for him. He has always been careful not to take things he wasn't sure he was offered.

"Did you kill the deceased?" Sal asks.

"Yes."

No one in the gallery makes a sound. I think they expected him to take longer.

"Why?"

"Because he asked me to," the accused says. "And because somebody had to."

"When did he first ask?"

"Six years ago. A little after the boy was born. In the car, at the signal on the main road." He speaks clearly, for the stenographer. "He was doing sums on the back of a fuel receipt. School, rent, the second-hand cot, the car. He'd done them three times and they kept coming out the same. He said, 'I can't do this.' I said, 'I can.'"

"And then?"

"Then we talked. Mornings, mostly. In traffic." He folds his hands on the rail. "That's why the window stayed up, if the court is wondering. We were in a meeting."

I never sat in that car with him. Write that down somewhere.

"How did it work, this arrangement?"

"Slowly. He'd give me an hour. Then evenings. Then the weekends. Thursdays were for tea with a friend, so Thursdays went early." He doesn't look at Sal when he says it. "He said his friend would understand."

Sal's ears have gone red, the way they did when we were fourteen. He turns a page he hasn't read.

"Did the family know?"

"They asked for me." For the first time there's something underneath his voice, like a floor under a carpet. "Every remark at every table was an invitation. Stand up straight. Other men manage. Look at your brother-in-law's car. Grown men don't play games. He put the games away himself. He was the one who wrapped the cable around the console." He looks toward the third row and then away. "It was decided that I would take over as head of the family. It was decided by everyone who ate at that table. I didn't break in. I was let in."

"And what did you give them?"

"Everything they asked for. A house with three bedrooms. Fees on the first of the month. A man who could stand beside her at her sister's without anyone looking at his shoes."

"And when did the deceased die?"

"The fourteenth of March, last year. A Tuesday. In the car." He says it the way you'd give a date of birth. "He said, 'Look after them.' And then he was quiet. And I drove to work."

"Fourteen months ago."

"Yes."

"And the family went to the police eight months ago."

"Yes." He straightens his cuff, though it doesn't need straightening. "It took them six months to notice he was gone. I'd like the court to remember that. I was good enough at it that it took them six months. And when they finally noticed, they didn't thank me. They called me a murderer and sent for the police."

"No further questions."

Hale stands. She still has no papers.

"Are you aware that consent is not a defence to murder?"

"I am now, ma'am."

"You've heard the letter. 'If I ever die, it was his fault.' If he asked you to do this, why did he blame you?"

"Because he loved them too much to blame them," the accused says. "Someone had to be in the letter."

"'I'm sorry I wasn't enough.' Did you think he was enough?"

"No."

"Did you ever tell him he was?"

He takes a moment. "That wasn't my job."

"Two hundred and twelve messages from defence counsel to the deceased. 'Tea? Usual place.' Every Thursday, for four years. The deceased read every one of them, and never answered. Was that his choice?"

"No," the accused says. "Mine. If he'd sat down across from his friend, he'd have changed his mind. It was too late in the plan for that."

"The last one says, 'I'll stop asking. Not because I'm angry. Because I think it's making you sad to say no.'" Hale lets the words settle. "Did it make him sad, saying no?"

The accused looks at the defence table. Sal is looking at his own hands.

"It makes him sad," the accused says.

Hale waits, but he doesn't correct himself.

"You have everything the family asked for," she says. "The house. The fees. The standing. Are they happy?"

The radiator knocks. He doesn't answer until it has finished.

"No."

"Are you?"

He looks at his watch. It's the first time he has looked at it all day.

"That wasn't the arrangement," he says.

"One last question. When did you last see Eli?"

"The fourteenth of March."

"You're sure?"

He glances at the third row. Not at Mira. At Sami, who has fallen asleep against his sister with his mouth open, exactly the way I used to sleep in the car.

"Yes," he says, a beat late.

"No further questions."

Hale gives her closing from the spot where she stood this morning. Her hands are empty.

"He tells you the deceased asked for this," she says. "He tells you the family asked for it. Perhaps they did. People ask for all sorts of things across a dinner table. Stand up straight. Earn more. Be someone I can stand next to." She glances, once, at the third row. "Asking a man to change is not asking him to die. A man may be asked to become more. He cannot agree to become nothing, not on behalf of a little girl who still had a game to finish with him."

She turns to the accused.

"There's a picture in every children's book. A man chasing a rainbow, because at the end of it there's a pot of gold. The accused chased it for six years. He was very good at it. Better than anyone. And when he finally got there, do you know what he found?"

She waits until the room is quiet enough to hear the radiator thinking about it.

"Breakfast," she says. "A kitchen table. Two children and a woman in a grey dress. The same table and the same people who were there when he started running. They were the gold. They were always the gold. And the only man who knew it was the man he killed."

She sits down.

Sal stands. He takes his time getting to the middle of the floor.

"My learned friend says asking isn't killing," he says. "She's right. The people who ask never hold the knife. That's what makes asking so comfortable. If this was murder, Your Honour, half this gallery should be sitting next to my client. They won't be. They'll go home tonight, and someone will put the kettle on."

He doesn't look at Mira. He doesn't need to.

"I'll tell you why I took this case," he says. "It wasn't because I think he's innocent. It was because of something he said today. Ms. Hale asked whether it made the deceased sad to say no to tea, and he said, 'It makes him sad.'" Sal lets that sit. "Not made. Makes. A man fourteen months dead, and he talks about him in the present tense. As if he's still in there to be sad."

He turns to the bench.

"Execute this man, and you kill the only one who knows where Eli is buried."

Then, more quietly, as if he's forgotten the court is listening:

"My last message said I'd stop asking. I didn't. Call this the two hundred and thirteenth." He touches the knot at his throat. "For twenty years he tied my tie before anything important. Today I tied it myself."

He sits down. The accused looks at Sal's tie, the thin, apologetic knot, for a long moment, and his hands move on the rail as if they remember something they've been told to forget.

In the third row, Sami has woken up. He sits up against Noor, rubs his eyes, and finds the accused across the room. Then he does what he did at two in the morning on the stairs, eight months ago. He lifts his arms.

Noor catches his wrist and pulls it down. But not before the accused's hand comes up off the rail, an inch, two inches, and stops in the air.

The judge is gone for forty minutes. Nobody leaves. Mira buys the children juice from the machine in the corridor and brings it back, and nobody opens it. Sal sits with his hands flat on the table. The accused sits exactly as he sat this morning, except that his jacket is still unbuttoned.

Since you've been patient, I'll tell you one thing while we wait.

There were mornings in the car. I'll give him that much. I didn't agree to anything. But I didn't get out, either.

And I'll tell you something else, so you don't go home hoping. The dead don't come back. Everyone knows that.

The side door opens. We all stand, and then we all sit, except one.

"Will the accused rise."

He rises. His hand goes to the button of his jacket, from habit, and then, for no reason I can see, it stops there and comes away.

The judge settles her glasses on her nose and reads without looking up.

"This court accepts that the deceased knew his killer for many years, and did not stop him. It accepts that others made the killing easier, and that some of them made it welcome. Neither is a defence. A man's agreement to his own disappearance is not an agreement the law recognises. Least of all when it was given in traffic, on the back of a fuel receipt."

She turns the page.

"The court finds Elias Marr guilty of the murder of Elias Marr."

She takes her glasses off.

"The sentence of this court is death. The date will be set."
